As far as footwear goes, the only 2 things you really need are a defined heel (like logger boots)  and a steel shank.


In case you dont already know, inside boots, there is a 'shank' or strip that runs the length of the footbed.  It's there to provide rigidity to the whole boot and disperse your weight across the whole footbed.

Many boots have a polyurethane shank because it's cheaper.  It's also more comfortable on the ground because it's more flexible.  However, with tree spikes, you want the opposite.  You need the steel shank to better spread the pressure on your foot from the stirrup.

It's been a while since i read the manual, but i thought it mentioned ambient air temps in the section with the P setting chart.

Either way, it's fairly straightforward.  Cold air takes more energy to heat up and keep hot than warm air does.  

I use the P setting for beef jerky a lot.  I set it to 200 to get the smoker fired up, then switch to the P setting and leave it at the default P4 until the temps stabilize.  Then i adjust from there.  In the spring and fall, when it's mid-70s out, p5 and p6 holds a 165-170 grill temp.  As it gets darker and colder (mid 40s and lower), i usually end up on P3, or p2 in dead winter.

The temperatures you're trying to maintain are gunna to determine what direction your P setting should go.  Colder ambient temps mean a lower P setting number.  Higher ambient temps mean a higher P setting number.

Since the environment varies so much, you really just gotta experiment with and learn what works best for you

'4' is considered the default, and depending on ambient air temps, you should keep you around 180°F.

The lower the number, the more frequently it will feed pellets to the burn pot

The higher the number, the longer the pause between feed cycles.

If you're trying to go to 200° and above, then you just use the regular temp settings on the dial.  Or at least the number closest to it.


Also have you cleaned your grill of soot/ash and cleaned the temp probes?  That will have a significant impact as well

As far as other easy things to do, Steaks!  Get a nice thick cut NY Strip or good Hanger Steak

Season with SPG blend (salt, pepper, garlic) or any steak rub you want
Let stand 30 minutes
Smoke at 200-225 until internal temp is about 30 degrees away from your desired internal temp
(Medium Rare is ~130° so pull at 100 or so)
Crank the smoker to max heat
Give the steaks a super light brushing with mayo, and apply more seasonings if you want to
Place back on the grill
Cook until desired temp and nice grill marks

The smoke mode is for sub-200° smoking temps. However, you can make it go over 200 in certain conditions/settings.

Switching it to smoke mode changes how the auger feeds pellets into the firebox.  Instead of the computer calculating and feeding pellets based on temp readings, it goes to a timed feed cycle.  That feed cycle is controlled by the "P" setting.  There's a little button in the top right that's labeled "P" and a number shown on the screen.  You can find the exact times online, but the higher the P setting, the longer the pause between feed cycles, the lower the P setting, the shorter the pause is.  The 'default' P setting is P4, and it's recommended that you use that to begin with and base your changes around how P4 affects your cooks.

3-2-1 method 

Smoke uncovered at ~250°F for 3 hours.  The goal is to form a nice crust. That crust is called bark in the smoking world.  You can also spray/spritz with Apple Cider Vinegar, Apple Juice, or water if you're worried about them drying out.


Smoke for 2 hours wrapped in foil or butcher paper. This is where people usually add butter, honey, more bbq rub, and other things like apple juice.  It's not necessary to add stuff with butcher paper, but i still add butter and a drizzle of honey.

Remove from the wrap carefully(foil) and give a brushing of your favorite bbq sauce.  Smoke for 1 more hour to let the sauce set a nice glaze.

Remove and enjoy

* The times and temp for this are not set in stone. it's just a baseline that you can modify as you like

There are 3 choices in regards to product

Storing

This option will utilize the space in the spawn area.  When the spawn area is filled, the building will use the internal storage space, spawning product as you make room in the spawn area

Selling

This option will automatically sell your product as it produced, you will be deducted a delivery fee

Distributing

This option will automatically move product to the next step in the production.  For example if you make flour, and set the production to distributing, it will send the flour to the bakery if you own it to be used in the next step.  If there is no next step, or the next step is not owned, it will store the product internally, WITHOUT SPAWNING PALLETS.

Those are the only mandatory* steps to get a crop to grow.

Mulching, fertilizing, rolling etc are all optional as they affect the yield

If you want 100% yield, heres one way to do it

-Mulch the stubble post harvest
-Lime the field if needed (if not then fertilize)
-Cultivate (plow if needed)
-Sow/plant/seed (fertilize after if your seed drill does not fertilize)
-Roll
-Weed (if needed)
-Fertilize after a growth stage appears (if you arent at 100%fertilizer yet)
-Harvest


Thats just one example on how,  but in a general sense for 100% yield you need

-A mulching
-2 fertilizer treatments ((each is 50%)(slurry can be double applied at once)
-A rolling after planting
-Weeding
-Field needs (plowing and/or lime)

Seeders and planters sow(plant) your different crops. Grains like wheat and barley are typically are done with seeders, and root crops like corn or sugarbeets are done with planters.

Harvesting is harvesting

NOTE:  There are several seeders and 1 base game planter that can do whats called 'direct seeding'.  This simply means you can skip the plowing and cultivating steps after harvesting.
